Excuse me, sorry to bother you. Could you tell me where the shuttle to the center stops?
Of course. It stops outside door four. Go straight ahead to the end of this hall, and then it is around the corner, on your left.
Thank you. Do you know if it still runs at this time? It is almost ten.
It runs until midnight, but after nine it only comes every forty minutes. The last one tonight leaves at eleven fifty.
Good, I have time then. Could you tell me how long it takes to the center?
About twenty-five minutes at this hour. Where are you heading to?
The Garden Hotel, on Garden Street. Do you know if it is far from the stop? I was wondering if I could go on foot.
Get off at the second stop and it is four minutes on foot, all flat. Take a picture of the address just in case. And if you get lost, everybody in that square knows the hotel.

My name is Martin, and I stand behind an information desk in a European airport, eleven hours a day, and I answer questions. Thousands of them. So let me tell you something that nobody tells travelers, and that costs nothing to learn. It is not your grammar that decides the answer you get from me. It is the first four words of your question. When somebody walks up and says, where is the shuttle, flat, like that, I answer in five seconds and I look at the next person. When somebody says, excuse me, could you tell me where the shuttle stops, I stop, I look up, and I tell them the stop, and the time, and that the second one is closer to their hotel, and that on Sunday it only runs every forty minutes. Same information desk. Same man. Same day. Two completely different answers. And here is the part that surprises people. Those four words are not about being polite for the sake of being polite. They are about time. Excuse me, could you tell me gives me one second to turn my head, and it tells me you are going to ask something real. I hear people with beautiful English get short answers, and I hear people with fifty words of English get my whole attention, because they opened the door before they walked through it. So if you are nervous about your English, do not spend the night before your trip studying verbs. Learn four openings by heart. Excuse me, could you tell me. Do you know if. Sorry to bother you. I was wondering if you could help me. Say them in the mirror until they come out without thinking, and every stranger in Europe becomes a person who wants to help you.

I am Teresa, I am sixty-nine, and I want to tell you about the strangest evening of my life. Two weeks before my first trip alone, I sat down in my kitchen in the evening and I did the whole journey out loud, in English, to nobody. My daughter thought I had lost my mind. I started at the gate. I said, excuse me, could you tell me if this is the gate for the two o'clock flight. Then I stood up, I walked to the door, and I was in the arrivals hall. I said, do you know where I can find a shuttle to the center. Then the street. Do you know if the hotel is far, can I go on foot. Then the front desk. Good evening, I have a reservation under Teresa. And I did it again the next night, and the night after that, until the sentences came out of my mouth by themselves, the way your telephone number does. It took forty minutes each time. Now, listen, because this is the part that matters. Three weeks later I was standing in a real airport, at ten at night, and the shuttle was not where the paper said it was. And I did not freeze. My mouth opened and the sentence came out, already made: excuse me, could you tell me where the shuttle stops now. A woman pointed around the corner, and I was at my hotel in twenty minutes. I did not need more English that night. I needed the sentences to be ready before I was scared. That is what a rehearsal is. You are not learning the words. You are putting them somewhere you can reach them with your hands shaking.
